r.x: Samuel Gawith
is living history in the world of pipe tobacco. The brand's roots go back to a tobacco and snuff works founded in 1792 in
Kendal

, a town in England's Lake District — a heritage the firm still proudly carries on its packaging today. Shaped over the centuries by family splits and mergers within Kendal's tobacco trade, the business has operated under a shared roof with its sister company
Gawith Hoggarth & Co.
since 2015.
Traditionalist Production
What sets Samuel Gawith apart is its production philosophy: the tobaccos are processed on presses and machines, some dating back to the Victorian era,
faithful to century-old recipes
. The brand's specialty is
flake
tobacco, steam-heated, pressed into blocks under high pressure, and then thinly sliced. This method gives the tobacco a dark, mature, and deep character.
Famous Blends
Full Virginia Flake (FVF):
Considered the world's benchmark for pure Virginia flakes, celebrated for its dried-fruit and bready sweetness.
Squadron Leader:
A balanced, refined English blend classic containing Latakia.
1792 Flake:
A strong, dark Kendal tradition flavored with tonka bean.
Availability

Labor-intensive production can't always keep up with demand; the occasional disappearance of Samuel Gawith tobaccos from the market has become something of a running joke in the pipe community. Despite this — or perhaps partly because of it — the brand's blends are among the most heavily cellared tobaccos in collectors' stashes.

r.x: Lane Limited

is a pipe tobacco maker, now headquartered in the United States, whose roots trace to Dresden, Germany, in 1890. Considered a defining force in shaping the American aromatic blend style, the company is known both for its globally recognized packaged Captain Black series and for its bulk blends identified by code names, chief among them 1-Q. Bulk tobacco refers to tobacco sold openly by weight rather than in packaged form; Lane is considered one of the world's best-known producers in this category. The company has operated under the Scandinavian Tobacco Group since 2011.
From Dresden to New York

The company was founded in Dresden in 1890 by the ancestors of the Lane family and specialized in pipe and roll-your-own tobaccos. The founder's grandson, Herman G. Lane, left Nazi Germany in 1938 to emigrate to the United States and re-established the business in Manhattan, New York. The company quickly took hold in its new home: its 1940s catalog listed forty different pipe blends.

Pipe tobaccos were produced in the Manhattan building for many years; according to records, production moved to a factory in Tucker, Georgia, around 1983. It's said that some employees were so devoted to the company that they chose to relocate with it from New York to Georgia.
Signature Blends

Lane's best-known brand is Captain Black, which first appeared in its 1956 catalog. Having grown over time into one of the world's most widely recognized packaged pipe tobaccos, this series is counted among the modern representatives of codger blends, the everyday American classics of the category.

The company's flagship on the bulk tobacco side is 1-Q. Built on a base of golden Virginia and black Cavendish with a note of vanilla, this blend has for decades been considered the best-selling bulk pipe tobacco in the US and the world. It is known that 1-Q has been relabeled under different names by various tobacconists, meaning the same blend also circulates under other names. Other code-named bulk blends such as BCA, RLP-6, and MV-1000 are likewise considered classics of the trade.
The American Aromatic Style and Today

By pairing a black Cavendish base with a sweet casing, Lane is regarded as the producer that set the standard for the American aromatic style. In this style, tobacco is defined less by its natural character than by the flavor and scent added to it; casing and flavoring techniques accordingly occupy a central place in the company's approach to blending. Light, sweet-profiled blends have become synonymous with the Lane name over time.

In March 2011, the Denmark-based Scandinavian Tobacco Group acquired Lane Limited; on June 1, 2012, the company's official name changed to "Scandinavian Tobacco Group Lane Ltd." Today the company continues to operate under the Scandinavian Tobacco Group, headquartered in Tucker.

r.x: Gawith Hoggarth & Co.

is a pipe tobacco and snuff maker operating in Kendal, Cumbria, on the edge of England's Lake District. The firm was founded in 1887 through the partnership of William Henry Gawith and Henry Hoggarth Jr., and took over the water mill at Helsington Laithes immediately after its founding. A present-day carrier of the Kendal tobacco-making tradition, whose roots reach back to 1792, the company shares a family tree with Samuel Gawith; it is known for its rope tobaccos, its dark fire-cured blends, and its distinctive "Lakeland" scent.
Family Tree and History

The firm's origin traces to Thomas Harrison, who went to Glasgow in 1792 to learn the tobacco trade. In 1805 Harrison founded a tobacco manufactory in Kendal called "Harrison & Brocklebank" with chemist Thomas Brocklebank. The business passed to the Gawith family when his granddaughter Jane married Samuel Gawith. In the nineteenth century, one branch that split off within the family continued under the name Samuel Gawith, while the partnership William Henry Gawith formed with Henry Hoggarth Jr. took the name Gawith Hoggarth & Co.

According to records, the family business operated from the building on Lowther Street in Kendal from the 1830s onward; the company moved to a modern facility in 1993. Management stayed within the family across generations: in the twentieth century Geoffrey Gawith, and then John Gawith, ran the firm; today it is headed by fourth-generation Rachel and Chris Gawith. In 2015 the two cousin-firms merged under one roof; in this way the Gawith branches that had split in the nineteenth century came back together in Kendal.
The Last Bearer of Traditional Formats

What sets Gawith Hoggarth apart is that it keeps alive production methods the tobacco industry has largely abandoned. Century-old machines and old-fashioned methods are still used in production today; the firm is counted among the last independent traditional producers of this scale left in England. Its main areas of expertise are as follows:
Rope tobaccos (rope/twist):
This old cut, obtained by twisting and winding the leaves like rope, is kept alive through products such as Rum Twist and Brown Bogie; the smoker rubs a slice cut from the rope before use.
Kendal Kentucky:
Strong, smoky blends based on Dark Fired Kentucky leaf, cured with wood-fire smoke, are among the firm's classics.
Snuff:
The production of snuff — tobacco reduced to a fine powder for nasal use — is one of the firm's oldest specialties, associated with its water-mill tradition.
Lakeland Scent

The signature most associated with the brand's name, however, is the "Lakeland scent." This floral, faintly soapy flavoring specific to the Lake District is applied to a range of blends; its best-known example is Ennerdale Flake, a pressed, thinly sliced tobacco. The Lakeland style is considered a distinct branch within aromatic blends and is known for sharply dividing lovers from haters with its pronounced character: some smokers consider the scent a nostalgic English classic, while others find it overpowering. It is also generally accepted that the style has remained largely confined to Kendal today.

r.x: Dunhill Pipe Tobacco Blends

are counted among the most respected English tobacco lines in the pipe world. Born from the tobacconist Alfred Dunhill opened in 1907 on Duke Street in London's St James's district, the series produced classics such as My Mixture 965, Nightcap, and Early Morning Pipe, considered the benchmark of their type. This entry covers only the brand's tobacco side; for the pipes known for their white spot, see Dunhill (White Spot).
The "My Mixture" Tradition

Alfred Dunhill presented himself as a "tobacco specialist." Rather than selling ready-made packets, his shop prepared a personal blend (mixture) to each customer's taste and recorded the recipe in a ledger titled "My Mixture." Records say these ledgers accumulated tens of thousands of personal recipes over time, and that customers included well-known literary figures and members of the court of the day. As the business grew, the most popular recipes began, from the early 1910s, to be entered into catalogs as ready-made packets; personal blends thus turned into standard products sold worldwide. The name of the line's flagship, My Mixture 965, also comes from this ledger tradition; the recipe is said to trace back to a blend prepared for a single customer before 1910.
The "Big Three"

When Dunhill comes up in the community, the first thing that comes to mind is the trio known as the "Big Three" English blends. Nightcap and Early Morning Pipe were introduced in 1951, while My Mixture 965 is distilled from a much older recipe. The three are considered steps on the same ladder in terms of Latakia proportion and strength:

rows: Heavy Latakia supported by Virginia, Oriental tobacco, and Perique; designed for the end of the day, full-bodied and strong
Latakia, Macedonian-sourced Oriental tobaccos, and brown Cavendish; round, full, and balanced
Oriental-forward, supported by lightly toasted Virginia; Latakia present only at a seasoning level

r.x: As their names imply, the trio is thought of as a family designed for different times of day: the lightest for morning, the darkest for night.
From Murray to Peterson

The blends were prepared at Dunhill's own facility in London until 1981. That year, production was handed to Murray, Sons & Co., a Belfast firm with roots going back to the early 19th century. When British American Tobacco (BAT) closed its Belfast factory at the end of 2004, production moved to Denmark, to the Orlik facility now part of the Scandinavian Tobacco Group (STG). When BAT withdrew entirely from the pipe tobacco and cigar business in 2018, Dunhill blends disappeared from world markets. STG announced in 2019 that it had bought the brand and design rights to the blends; in November of that year, classics including Nightcap, Early Morning Pipe, Mixture 965, and Royal Yacht went back into production under the Peterson label. Since production had already been running for years at the same Danish factory, the recipes are considered unchanged. Old Dunhill tins, meanwhile, have become pieces cellared and aged in collectors' stores, spoken of with respect among enthusiasts.

r.x: Cornell & Diehl

(C&D for short) is regarded as one of the most prolific names in American boutique pipe tobacco blending. Started by Craig and Patty Tarler as a retirement pursuit, the firm is known for its small-batch approach, an unusually wide range of blends, and hands-on methods. The brand name comes from combining Craig's middle name, Cornell, with Patty's maiden name, Diehl.
Founding and Growth

The firm was born in the early 1990s — sources give the founding year variously as 1990 to 1992 — through the purchase of the inventory of a closing blending house called Amar Blending Company. Production first ran out of the Tarlers' garage in Pennsylvania, then, after 1994, out of a garage in Morganton, North Carolina; the brand did not get its first true production facility until 2005.

Following Craig Tarler's death in 2012, the company merged in 2014 with Laudisi Enterprises, the parent organization of Smokingpipes.com, and moved to South Carolina. The brand moved to its current facility near Longs in 2023; the company's history notes that production volume grew many times over under Laudisi, without the small-batch approach being abandoned.
Production Philosophy

What sets C&D apart is that it has kept hands-on craftsmanship as it has scaled up: blends are prepared in small quantities to order, mixed and pressed by hand. This approach both keeps the tobacco fresh and allows the firm to keep hundreds of different blends alive at once. As against large factories' single-type, high-volume production, the C&D catalog offers a wide variety that reflects the experimental curiosity left over from the garage days; in this respect the brand is counted among the pioneers of the American "boutique blending" movement.

The firm has also been the manufacturer of every blend carrying the G.L. Pease label since 2000; the two brands' partnership, spanning more than a quarter century, is considered the best-known collaboration in American boutique blending.
Notable Blends
Star of the East:
A dark-character English blend in which Cyprus Latakia makes up roughly half the mix, rounded out with Izmir Oriental tobacco and red Virginia.
Bayou Morning:
A spicy Virginia-Perique blend with a high proportion of Perique.
Autumn Evening:
A maple-flavored blend, the brand's best-known aromatic.
Small Batch series:
Limited yearly special releases, such as Carolina Red Flake, known for quickly selling out among collectors.

The brand also has a notable angle from a Turkish perspective: C&D gives Oriental leaf — Izmir foremost among them — a place in many of its English-type blends. This choice is cited as an example of Turkish tobacco's visibility in contemporary American blending.

r.x: G.L. Pease

is the American boutique pipe tobacco brand founded by blending master Gregory L. Pease at the start of 2000 in California. The brand's founding purpose is to keep alive the classic English blend style that was fading with industrialization; this approach is summed up in the slogan "Preindustrial Tobaccos for the Contemporary Pipe Smoker." With a model that pairs small-scale design thinking with large-scale manufacturing, G.L. Pease is considered one of the pioneers of the boutique blending movement that rose in the 2000s.
From Drucquer & Sons to His Own Brand

Pease learned the trade at Drucquer & Sons, a shop legendary in pipe circles in Berkeley, California. A regular there during his university years, he later began working at the shop and personally prepared its famous house blends. As the account goes, Drucquer & Sons was an established business with a reach wide enough to receive order letters from Admiral Byrd's polar team and director Cecil B. DeMille; Pease is considered a carrier of that tradition.

Before his own brand, he founded "Friedman & Pease" in 1998 with his friend Irwin Friedman as a first venture. This partnership, which lasted about eighteen months, became the forerunner of G.L. Pease Tobaccos, which he founded on his own at the start of 2000.
Production Model

One of the brand's most notable features is its production model. Pease develops the blend recipes himself; mass production has been handled since 2000 by Cornell & Diehl. This division of labor — design at a boutique blender, production at an established factory — is regarded as one of the first major examples of the boutique-design-plus-contract-manufacturing partnership that later became common in the pipe tobacco world. This model has made it possible for a small brand to reach a wide audience without compromising on its recipes.
Blends and Collections
G.L. Pease publishes its blends in thematic collections such as Original Mixtures, Classic Collection, Fog City Selection, and Old London Series. Its notable examples can be listed as follows:
Westminster:
Considered the textbook example of the classic English mixture.
Blackpoint:
Brings together red and lemon Virginia leaf with Cyprus-sourced Latakia, Oriental tobaccos, and Perique.
Abingdon, Quiet Nights, Maltese Falcon, Gaslight:
Cited among the most highly rated contemporary English and Balkan blends in user reviews.
Writing and Influence

Pease is known not only for his blends but for his writing on pipe tobacco. His "Briar & Leaf Chronicles" pieces on his own site and his column in Pipes Magazine are among the most frequently referenced texts on tobacco varieties, blend construction, and aging; he is counted among the field's most cited writers in this respect. The brand continues to release new blends today, preserving its role as a bridge between the classic English style and today's pipe smoker.

r.x: McClelland Tobacco Company

was a pipe tobacco manufacturer operating in Kansas City, Missouri, from 1977 to 2018. Regarded as the world's reference brand in matured Virginia, the company became one of the most talked-about names in American pipe culture, thanks to its whale emblem and the distinctive tangy smell of its tins.
Founding and Rise

The brand's origin traces to Carl R. Ehwa Jr. joining Kansas City's well-known tobacconist Fred Diebel in 1969. There Ehwa developed blends for the shop and was put in charge of a small manufactory attached to it; he gathered the knowledge from these years into a book,
The Book of Pipes and Tobaccos

, published by Random House/Ridge Press in 1974. The company was founded in 1977 by Ehwa, his wife Mary, and Ehwa's childhood friend Bob Berish Jr. (given as Benish in some sources). Production began in the basement of the home of Ehwa's grandfather, Dr. W.C. McClelland, the man the company was named after; Dr. McClelland, who died at 87, took part in the preparations but never saw the first sale. The company launched with ten blends, five Oriental mixtures and five matured Virginias.

When Berish left in 1980, Mike McNiel, who had previously worked with Ehwa at the Diebel manufactory, joined the staff. In 1982, at thirty-six, Ehwa suffered a brain aneurysm and was unable to return to run the company; the business stayed afloat through the shared efforts of a small staff that included sales manager Marv Novy. Mary and Mike McNiel, who ran the company together, married in 1993. When the factory eventually spread through the whole of the McClelland house, an insurance company warning prompted a move in 1985: the new address was a hundred-year-old building in Kansas City's arts district, whose upper floor, it was later learned, had been used as a speakeasy in the 1920s.
Tins and Packaging

In the early years, tins were sealed with paper wrap and hot wax. According to the founders' account, this was meant both to give a traditional look and to disguise the fact that the tin could only be opened with a can opener. The choice of American-made tins limited their options; they were only able to switch to an easy-open pop-top tin in the early 1980s. This distinction is one of the criteria used to roughly date remaining old tins. Label color was another marker: matured Virginias came out with a brown label, Oriental mixtures with green. Mary McNiel drew the artwork on some of the tins, including the Frog Morton series.
Blends and Style

McClelland's name is above all associated with matured Virginia. After the first ten blends, the product range expanded with private-label series prepared for bulk sale at tobacconists' blending counters, as well as aromatics. The tangy, ketchup-like smell noticed on opening the tins became synonymous with the brand; fans attribute this smell to natural Virginia fermentation, though the company never gave a definitive explanation of its source.
The brand's most talked-about products are as follows:
Christmas Cheer:

Prepared in 1992 as a one-off product for the company's fifteenth anniversary, it became a permanent fixture given the interest it drew, with each year's batch made from a different harvest — a series that turned into a tradition of collectors aging and comparing vintages.
Frog Morton series:
Counted among the best-known American interpretations of the English style through its mellow Latakia-containing blends.
5100 Red Cake:
One of the most frequently cited red Virginia blends in the American pipe community.
Grand Orientals:

A series presenting Ottoman-region Oriental tobacco varieties one by one in pure form — Yenice (Yenidje), Smyrna No. 1, Drama Reserve, and Katerini Classic — considered unique for documenting the heritage of Türkiye's tobacco regions and Balkan tobacco culture.
A break in the aging tradition is also on record: in 1993, Christmas Cheer was not released because suitable leaf could not be set aside in time; the series resumed the following year.
Levin Blends and Cigar Experiments

The brand's path crossed in 1989 with Barry Levin, the Vermont dealer considered the pioneer of the American estate pipe trade. Levin would send Kansas City the twenty-, thirty-, and forty-year-old tins that came his way along with the pipe collections he bought, and ask for similar versions of these old tobaccos to be made. These requests led to tobaccos first produced under private label for Levin's company; after Levin's death in 1994, McClelland added them to its own catalog under the names Personal Reserve and Craftsbury. The Craftsbury name comes from Levin's Vermont town.

The curiosity sparked by the cigar craze of the early 1990s led the company to work with cigar leaf as well. Dominican Glory and Dominican Glory Maduro were the product of experiments adapting this leaf to a pipe's moisture and burning conditions. The same effort produced the Ballena Suprema cigar series, rolled for the company in Honduras and Mexico.
Closure and Legacy

The company announced its closure in February 2018. Among the reasons cited were the McNiels' advancing age, Mike McNiel's health problems, the burden of US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulations, and the fact that Virginia leaf suited to the brand's old-fashioned processes could no longer be found. The founders pointed to the replacement of small farmers — who once entered the field several times to hand-pick only fully ripe leaf — by mechanical harvesting, and to the standardization of leaf after the quota and price-support system in the US was dismantled by the 2004 law, as the reason the subtle differences they sought had disappeared. Believing the company's name and reputation mattered more than money, the couple chose to close the firm rather than sell it; the recipes were handed to no one.

After the closure, the remaining tins became collector's items; the brand's blends are still cited as a benchmark in the pipe community. According to the founders, the whale emblem symbolized the beauty of the work done and the rarity of quality leaf.

r.x: Esoterica Tobacciana

is a pipe tobacco brand made at the J.F. Germain & Son factory on the Channel Island of Jersey, but built for the United States market. The brand owns no factory of its own: the blends are prepared at Germain's facilities under the brand's private label. This arrangement makes Esoterica a blending and distribution brand rather than a manufacturer.
The Brand's Origin

The factory behind the brand is, according to records, a tobacco house founded on Jersey in 1820 and kept within the same family across generations; it took its present name in the 1920s. The family name became attached to the firm when the founder's nephew, also named Germain, joined the business. For a long time Germain prepared private-label blends for other firms, part of which entered the American market under different names. The factory also continues to make blends under its own name; hence there are said to be two separate brand lines coming out of the same plant.

The Esoterica name was put forward by Steve Richman, who ran a tobacconist's shop in Oakland, California. As the account goes, while looking for a factory to produce the blends of his own choosing, Richman made contact with Germain and began importing these tobaccos under the name Esoterica Tobacciana. The exact start date is uncertain: sources place it anywhere from the mid-1980s to 1990. The names of the blends were drawn largely from British coastal towns: Penzance, Margate, Dorchester, Brighton, Scarborough, Tilbury, Dunbar, Blackpool. The one exception to this rule is "...And So To Bed," a blend conceived for the evening pipe.

Distribution rights later changed hands. Unable to build a wide distribution network on his own, Richman transferred the rights to Butera Pipe Company. In 2009 Butera's tobacco division passed to an American distributor, and Esoterica blends have continued to be made at Germain even after this change.
Blends

The Esoterica catalog falls into three main clusters. The first cluster consists of Latakia- and Oriental-forward mixtures belonging to the English blend tradition; Penzance, Margate, and Pembroke are the best-known examples of this group. The second cluster consists of Virginia-based blends, and the third of lightly flavored mixtures. Stonehaven stands apart on its own, as the only blend in the catalog containing burley.

Penzance is known as a flake tightly pressed and cut into thick slices; the scattered, crumbly structure of the slices is one of the brand's most talked-about features. The blends are packaged both in small tins and larger pouches; this second format has become popular among those who prefer long-term aging.
Supply and Reputation

Germain's insistence on traditional methods limits production volume; combined with the brand shipping only at certain times, this has made Esoterica blends hard to find in the pipe community. This scarcity has, in particular, driven a long-standing habit of stockpiling and aging around Penzance and Stonehaven. The brand remains in production today; but the irregularity of supply is cited as the main factor keeping curiosity about the name alive.

r.x: Mac Baren

, founded in the Danish town of Svendborg, is one of the world's most recognized pipe tobacco makers. Run by the Halberg family across generations, the company became synonymous with the fame earned by the blend series it took its name from; the 1958 Mixture blend became the brand's signature. With products reaching more than eighty countries, the firm joined the Scandinavian Tobacco Group (STG) under an agreement announced in June 2024.
The Halberg Family and the Birth of the Brand

The company's origins trace to a tobacco workshop opened by Svend Bønnelycke in Svendborg in 1826. In 1887, Harald Halberg bought the workshop and turned it into a modern tobacco factory under the name "Harald Halberg Tobaks- og Cigarfabrik"; the company also takes 1887 as its founding year. Leadership later passed to Harald's son Einar Halberg, and then to Harald's grandson Jørgen Halberg. It was Jørgen Halberg who created the "Mac Baren" blend series that gave the brand its name; once that series became the most successful product in the company's history, the firm officially took the name Mac Baren Tobacco Company in 1995.
Signature Blends and Production Philosophy

The brand's flagship, Mixture, launched in April 1958; according to the company's own history, it captured roughly a quarter of the Danish pipe tobacco market within three years. This blend, which brings together more than thirty-five different tobacco leaves, remains the company's best-known product today. Other signature products include Golden Extra, Navy Flake, prepared in a pressed flake cut, and Virginia No. 1, named for its Virginia leaf.

Mac Baren's production philosophy rests on light casing that doesn't mask the leaf's natural character. Launched in 2006 and named after founder Harald Halberg's initials, the HH series is considered the purest expression of this "let the tobacco speak for itself" approach. The series' best-known members are HH Old Dark Fired, built on fire-cured Dark Fired Kentucky leaf, and HH Vintage Syrian, which contains smoke-cured Syrian Latakia.
From Family Firm to STG

Between 2013 and 2015, the company expanded its presence in the US market by acquiring Altadis U.S.A.'s pipe tobacco division and the established American manufacturer Sutliff Tobacco Company. Long known as one of Northern Europe's largest family-owned tobacco producers, Mac Baren saw that era come to an end with the acquisition agreement announced in June 2024: leaving behind 137 years of family-company history, the firm came under the umbrella of the Scandinavian Tobacco Group. Under the announced restructuring plans, moving production from Svendborg to the Assens plant in Denmark and closing Sutliff's Richmond facility were put on the table; sources differ on the exact timeline of the process.

r.x: Sutliff Tobacco

is counted among the oldest pipe tobacco concerns in the United States. According to industry profiles, it was opened by H. W. Sutliff in 1849 in San Francisco as a tobacco and cigar shop, and over time grew into a manufactory blending its own recipes. The brand kept its corporate identity even after it passed out of the hands of the family whose name it bears, and it was known throughout the twentieth century especially for its bulk-sold blends.
From California to Virginia

The company's early years were spent in retail; according to industry sources, its true manufacturing phase began in 1933 with the launch of Mixture 79, a name still known today. This cube-cut burley-based blend quickly turned from a local product into a nationally recognized name, becoming the core product that kept the company alive for the long haul.

In 1953 the facilities and management moved to Richmond, Virginia. The reason for the move was to be closer to the tobacco leaf and cut shipping costs; Richmond was at the time one of the main centers of the American tobacco trade. Sutliff's production continued in this city for more than seventy years afterward. The factory's first form was designed largely around the manufacture of a single blend, to meet demand.
Changes of Ownership

Fourth-generation Gordon Sutliff handed the company over to Consolidated Cigar Corporation in 1969. When Consolidated joined Altadis U.S.A. in 2000, Sutliff too became part of this large structure. In 2013 the Danish family company Mac Baren bought Altadis U.S.A.'s pipe tobacco division; the Sutliff name was kept and the Richmond factory continued operating. In this period Sutliff also took over the distribution of Mac Baren products across the Americas.

The final change of hands came in 2024: the Scandinavian Tobacco Group took over Mac Baren, and with it, Sutliff. According to trade press reports, production in Richmond stopped on February 28, 2025, and only part of the catalog was moved to the group's facility in Denmark. What happens to the brand name and the rest of the recipes after this date has been left to decisions made within the group.
Its Place in the Bulk Market

Sutliff's recognition comes less from a single flagship product than from its broad catalog. The company was one of the main sources of "bulk" blends shipped to tobacconists in kilo-weight boxes rather than jars or packets; a trade profile from the Mac Baren era puts the catalog size at roughly two hundred fifty recipes. This catalog ran from vanilla- and cocoa-scented aromatic blends to plain Virginia recipes, from soft mixtures worked with Cavendish processing to burley-based classics.

This structure gave Sutliff a special place in American pipe tobacco making: the contents of many unnamed jars on local shop shelves were in fact Sutliff production. This is also why it is often mentioned alongside Lane Limited, which worked the same field; in the community's common view, these two houses are considered the country's main suppliers of the bulk tobacco tradition. Although no measured market-share figure exists, the halt of Richmond production was seen as the end not just of a brand but of a shelf arrangement familiar for decades.
